claim: Steam machines will erase nature, tranquility and human labour, leaving an unnatural world
what_happened: Industrial life brought vastly higher living standards, though real environmental costs arrived later
lesson: A vision of the future built from dread gets the costs half right and the benefits entirely wrong.

quotes.text: All things seemed forced, unnatural, unreal - indeed, little better than barefaced impositions.
quotes.speaker: Anonymous dreamer

claim: Human flight is a chimera that could take a million to ten million years
what_happened: The Wright Brothers flew nine weeks after the NYT piece
lesson: Visible failed attempts are evidence of difficulty, not of impossibility; false fails pile up right before the breakthrough.

quotes.text: To the ordinary man, it would seem as if effort might be employed more profitably
quotes.speaker: The New York Times

quotes.text: There probably can be found no better example of the speculative tendency carrying man to the verge of the chimerical than in his attempts to imitate the birds
quotes.speaker: George W. Melville

claim: Once flight worked, it would remain a plaything only the very rich could afford
what_happened: Air travel became mass transport within a few decades
lesson: Early products are expensive toys for the rich; price falls are the rule, not the exception.

quotes.text: the expense would be prohibitive to any but the capitalist who could use his own yacht.
quotes.speaker: William H. Pickering

thing: Free public libraries and cheap books
claim: Free libraries and cheap abundant books corrupt children with bad novels
what_happened: Public libraries became a civic good; childhood reading is now encouraged
lesson: The access-expanding thing gets blamed for whatever the newly reached audience does with it.

quotes.text: ...that makes the wholesale establishment of free public libraries almost as much a menace to the well-being of the country as would be the opening up of free saloons or opium joints
quotes.speaker: Dorothy Dix

quotes.text: the existence of all these books creates a restless spirit.
quotes.speaker: unnamed speaker

quotes.text: School-boys or students who took to novel reading to any great extent never made much progress in after life.
quotes.speaker: The New York Times

claim: Homes are over-lit and the new abundance of light is injuring our eyes
what_happened: Electric lighting became universal with no epidemic of eye injury
lesson: A health warning attached to abundance usually measures discomfort with change, not harm.

quotes.text: Our houses are overlighted
quotes.speaker: newspaper tips column

claim: The Statue of Liberty is killing birds
what_happened: Birds do collide with structures, but the toll never justified stopping them; the same argument now targets wind turbines
lesson: A real but small harm becomes the headline objection when the true objection is unfamiliarity.

claim: An expensive touchscreen phone with no keyboard would not sell
what_happened: The iPhone redefined the phone market and Microsoft lost mobile
lesson: Incumbents judge a new product by the old category's criteria, which is exactly what it is redefining.

quotes.text: ...it doesn't appeal to business customers because it doesn't have a keyboard. Which makes it not a very good email machine.
quotes.speaker: Steve Ballmer

claim: Families are dangerously dependent on TV and children read less because of it
what_happened: TV became universal; heavy viewing does correlate with less reading, but the predicted generational ruin did not happen
lesson: Screen-time panics recur on cue with every medium; the real effects are smaller and narrower than the headlines.

quotes.text: I guess many of us think we are intelligent enough to be independent of TV without quite realizing how much we rely on it.
quotes.speaker: anonymous parent

claim: Heavy radio listening damages hearing ("boiler factory ears")
what_happened: No hearing epidemic from radio; the claim was speculation with a doctor's title on it
lesson: A credentialed quote is not data; ask what the expert actually measured.

quotes.text: boiler factory ears
quotes.speaker: unnamed doctor

claim: Reading is an addictive craze, a dangerous stimulant
what_happened: Mass literacy and reading are now treated as unambiguous goods
lesson: Today's unquestioned virtue was often yesterday's addiction; the label tracks novelty, not harm.

quotes.text: Reading is a kind of craze that has gotten hold of the people. It is a dangerous habit, like a stimulant.
quotes.speaker: Former president of Johns Hopkins University

quotes.text: You enter a railway compartment and every one is reading, even the travelers on the dim “Underground” taxing their sight.
quotes.speaker: British Lord

claim: Reading on a moving railway train seriously injures the eyes
what_happened: Commuter reading (then phone use) became normal with no such injury epidemic
lesson: Health panics attach to the new posture of a habit; check whether harm was ever measured.

quotes.text: Such practices lead to serious injury to the eyes.
quotes.speaker: newspaper

claim: Reading in bed is a disease, as bad as drug taking
what_happened: Reading in bed is ordinary; the Spectator mocked the Daily Mail for stoking it
lesson: Fear sells papers; a health scare in a tabloid is a business model before it is a finding.

quotes.text: Reading in bed is a disease
quotes.speaker: doctor quoted in the Daily Mail

quotes.text: The habit is as bad as drug taking
quotes.speaker: doctor quoted in the Daily Mail

claim: Novel reading turns children into criminals, strikers and suicides
what_happened: Novel reading was later found harmless and is now encouraged; the cycle moved to film, radio, comics, TV, games
lesson: When bad things happen people blame the newest thing in the room; that is a pattern, not an explanation.

quotes.text: He comes from a good family, but he yearned to be a bandit.
quotes.speaker: The New York Times

claim: Young people are addicted to the new communication medium
what_happened: Each medium (tin-can phones, telegrams, telephone, texting) became mundane; the next one inherited the label
lesson: Communication is a core human need; a tool that makes it easier will always look "addictive" to outsiders.

claim: Holdouts said they would not have a radio in the house
what_happened: The holdouts bought radios as fast as they could
lesson: The loudest refusers are often late adopters, not non-adopters; do not read early resistance as a ceiling.

quotes.text: Those who “wouldn’t have one the things in the house” are now getting them in as soon as possible
quotes.speaker: newspaper

claim: Doctors push vaccination only to make money seeing more patients
what_happened: Vaccination eradicated smallpox; the profit-motive attack migrated to "big pharma"
lesson: A profit motive is not evidence a product does not work; attack the outcome data, not the margin.

claim: There could be no use for as many as forty-seven electronic brains
what_happened: Billions of computers exist
lesson: Early demand estimates are anchored on early use cases; new tools create the uses that size the market.

claim: Moving pictures cause juvenile crime
what_happened: Film became universal; the judge who defended it noted as many offenders came straight from church
lesson: The people loudest about a new medium often compete with it for the same hours of attention.

quotes.text: I have had twice that many cases of children who have been attending church and sunday school just before they commit their offenses.
quotes.speaker: juvenile court judge

claim: Women riding bicycles, in bloomers, is sinful and unwomanly
what_happened: Women won the sartorial culture war; cycling became a symbol of emancipation
lesson: When a product frees a group from a constraint, expect the backlash to be framed as morality.

quotes.text: Satan inspires women to ride wheels.
quotes.speaker: a doctor

claim: Bicycles cause accidents by scaring horses
what_happened: Bicycles were routinely blamed for accidents they did not cause; horses left the roads instead
lesson: A new thing on the road inherits the blame for every accident near it until the data says otherwise.

quotes.text: I should not have troubled you with this letter had it not been that bicycles are often blamed as the cause of accidents of which they are innocent–I am.
quotes.speaker: Scottish cyclist, letter to the editor

claim: Electricity is fine for phones and streetcars but cannot be trusted to cook
what_happened: Housewives came round from 1921; electric ovens became standard
lesson: Trust in a technology is domain-specific; win the high-stakes domestic use case and the rest follows.

quotes.text: Electricity may be all right for the telephone, the telegraph and the street car, but–well, really, I wouldn’t trust it with one of my cakes in the oven.
quotes.speaker: fictional housewife in newspaper

claim: A horseless carriage is more dangerous because it lacks the intelligence of the horse
what_happened: Cars did bring huge road deaths, but also displaced the horse; the same argument now shapes self-driving debates
lesson: A safety fear can be right about harm and wrong about adoption at the same time.

quotes.text: We should not overlook the fact that the driving of a horseless carriage calls for a larger amount of attention for he has not the advantage of the intelligence of the horse in shaping his path
quotes.speaker: Alfred Sennette

claim: Comic books cause juvenile delinquency
what_happened: Wertham's data was later shown to be manipulated; comics became mainstream culture, though a UK ban and US code followed
lesson: A single charismatic expert can launch a ban; check whether anyone else can reproduce the numbers.

quotes.text: The is no scientific proof that comics cause child delinquency.
quotes.speaker: Dr. F. W. Connell

quotes.text: Dr. Wethham's statistic prove beyond doubt that comic books do contribute to delinquency.
quotes.speaker: newspaper editorial

quotes.text: cannot afford the calculated risk involved in feeding its children, through comic books, a concentrated diet of crime, horror, and violence.
quotes.speaker: US Senate Judiciary subcommittee

claim: The Michelangelo virus would wipe millions of PCs
what_happened: The virus hit a few thousand machines; the panic made John McAfee rich selling antivirus
lesson: Whoever sells the cure has a stake in the size of the threat.

claim: The internet is a stupid fad that will collapse
what_happened: Bob Metcalfe literally ate his 1995 collapse prediction in 1997; a 1999 columnist admitted defeat
lesson: A Cambrian explosion of low-quality early content is the sign of democratized creation, not of a fad.

claim: There are too many writers and books; readers cannot consume it all
what_happened: Publishing output kept growing for over a century
lesson: "Too much content" is a complaint about filters, not production; the business is in the filter.

quotes.text: The reading world is not large enough to consume all that reading matter.
quotes.speaker: newspaper

claim: Modern art's ugliness is responsible for much of the horror in the world
what_happened: Modern art became the canon and sells for millions
lesson: Gatekeepers of the old form are the least reliable judges of the new one.

quotes.text: Great harm has been wrought in the world by the degeneracy of modern art.
quotes.speaker: art expert

claim: Television signals a lazy age; our hardy forefathers did without
what_happened: TV became universal; the "hardship was better" trope recurs with every jump in living standards
lesson: Nostalgia for hardship is a reliable sign that living standards just jumped.

quotes.text: Our forefathers had to carry water in pails; chop their own firewood to keep themselves warm
quotes.speaker: newspaper columnist

quotes.text: It is one more indication that the machine age will coddle man in the lap of luxury until he is unable to stand on his own feet
quotes.speaker: St. Joseph News-Press

claim: The labor-saving house is a Frankenstein monster that leaves the housewife alone with machines
what_happened: Appliances freed huge amounts of domestic labour
lesson: Cynicism about "labor saving" ignores the hours actually saved; measure the hours.

quotes.text: A housewife is alone and on her own with a veritable Frankenstein monster, which inventors have jokingly nicknamed the “labor saving” house.
quotes.speaker: newspaper

claim: Online adult content requires federal censorship of the internet
what_happened: The Communications Decency Act was struck down in 1997; concern about kids and online porn persists and is returning in state law
lesson: Regulation drafted in a panic tends to be struck down; the underlying concern often outlives the law.

claim: Pinball is an addictive gambling vice that ruins marriages; states banned it
what_happened: Bans (e.g. New York until 1976) were lifted; pinball is a nostalgic hobby
lesson: Bans on the hot new vice age into curiosities; the energy moves to the next device.

claim: The canal is not commercially viable or worth the money
what_happened: It became one of the most important trade routes in the world
lesson: Infrastructure is judged on today's traffic; it creates tomorrow's.

claim: Kodak management saw the digital camera as a threat to film and told its inventor to keep quiet
what_happened: Digital did destroy film; Kodak, which invented it, went bankrupt in 2012
lesson: When insiders fear a technology will cannibalize them, the fear is usually right; suppressing it only hands the market to someone else.

quotes.text: Don’t tell anyone about it.
quotes.speaker: Kodak management (as recalled by Steven Sasson)

claim: Vaccination produces more disease and death than smallpox itself
what_happened: Vaccination eradicated smallpox by 1980; a man who refused it while his family tested it died of smallpox in 1904
lesson: Rare side effects get headlines; the counterfactual deaths never do.

quotes.text: cannot the medical men see that the system of Jenner is an utter failure, that more disease and death is produced through its adoption than by small-pox in its natural form.
quotes.speaker: anti-vaccination letter

quotes.text: One might suppose that the popular prejudice against vaccination might have died out by this time, considering it has been practice for nearly a century
quotes.speaker: The New York Times

claim: High speed prevents people from exhaling carbon dioxide properly
what_happened: Untrue for the same reason you do not move backwards jumping in a plane
lesson: Speed-based health fears recur with every faster vehicle; physics usually answers them in a sentence.

claim: Developing hydro power in a coal-rich country is suicidal folly and kills jobs
what_happened: Hydro became a major clean power source; the same arguments now meet wind and solar
lesson: When the warning comes from the industry being replaced, discount it accordingly.

quotes.text: Developing of hyrdo-electric power in a country with adequate coal reserves is ‘suicidal folly.'
quotes.speaker: energy industry representative

quotes.text: Such a development is a modern Frankenstein. Hydro is our worst employer.
quotes.speaker: energy industry representative

claim: High-speed motoring elongates the brain and drives motorists insane
what_happened: No motoring insanity epidemic
lesson: A vivid mechanism (a stretched brain) is not evidence; ask for patients.

quotes.text: motor maniacs will be represented in the insane asylums in the near future.
quotes.speaker: brain specialist

claim: The telephone is a tool for love-smitten fools to gush over the wires
what_happened: Phone courtship became normal; the complaint migrated to texting and dating apps
lesson: Courtship always moves to the newest channel; the moralizing follows it there.

quotes.text: The telephone is invaluable to love-smitten fools of both sexes as a transmitter of soft taffy and gush when both parties know how to use the wires.
quotes.speaker: Chicago Tribune

claim: Edison has invented too many things
what_happened: A year later he perfected the lightbulb
lesson: "Too much innovation" complaints arrive just before the inventions that matter most.

quotes.text: Mr. Edison has invented too many things
quotes.speaker: The New York Times

claim: Electricity's subtle force shrinks heads and rots bones
what_happened: A delusion of its day, echoed by 5G conspiracies
lesson: Invisible forces attract invented harms; expect conspiracy, and answer with plain demonstration.

quotes.text: Possessed of the idea that his head has been decreased in size and the bones of his body rotted away through the subtle force of electricity...
quotes.speaker: newspaper

claim: GMO produce is dangerous Frankenfood (protesters picketed Jurassic Park)
what_happened: Scientific consensus finds approved GMOs safe, though European backlash restricted them for decades
lesson: A blockbuster story can set public opinion on a technology for a generation; manage the narrative early.

claim: Jazz causes crime, suicide, bad grades and moral decay
what_happened: Jazz became American classical music
lesson: Do not render curses to the newest trend for every ill of the empire.

quotes.text: Let us not render curses to Caesar for every ill that befalls the empire
quotes.speaker: newspaper columnist

claim: Unregulated "video nasties" on VHS corrupt children
what_happened: A tabloid panic produced the 1984 Video Recordings Act; home video became universal
lesson: A new distribution channel that escapes existing censorship triggers a moral panic until it is brought under the old rules.

claim: Crossword puzzles distract students and must be banned from class
what_happened: Crosswords became a respected pastime; the complaint moved to laptops and phones
lesson: Educators ban whatever competes with the lecture; competing better is the durable fix.

claim: D&D is essentially a worship of violence and corrupts youth
what_happened: D&D is mainstream culture and a recognized social hobby
lesson: A game that asks players to imagine is easy to paint as dangerous by people who have not played it.

quotes.text: essentially a worship of violence
quotes.speaker: Dr. Thomas Radecki

claim: Pagers in school help students deal drugs and should be banned
what_happened: Pagers were tied to drug trade in some places, but no student was caught; the fight moved to phones
lesson: A device that is genuinely used by bad actors still mostly serves ordinary users; ban the act, not the device.

quotes.text: I can’t say any student has ever been caught in the act.
quotes.speaker: school spokesman

claim: Kids are addicted to Pac-Man like gambling; age limits needed
what_happened: Gaming became universal; a small share of heavy players show problematic use, but the predicted generational damage never came
lesson: Addiction framing can be right for a minority while wrong for the median user; design for both.

claim: Amazon will go bankrupt and never again approach its $600 share price
what_happened: Amazon became one of the most valuable companies in the world
lesson: A crashed share price measures sentiment, not the business; companies that fail usually do so slowly, and so do the ones that win.

quotes.text: Amazon.com will never again approach its early 2000 share price of nearly $600, and there’s no guarantee the company will make a profit anytime soon.
quotes.speaker: newspaper

claim: The space race and moonshot are a frightful waste of public money ("moondoggle")
what_happened: A 1961 Gallup poll found 58% opposed; Apollo succeeded anyway, and only 20 years later did 77% say it was worth it
lesson: Before something works it is impossible; after it works it is an extravagant waste; neither verdict should stop a builder.

quotes.text: Anybody who would spend $40 billion in a race to the moon for national prestige is nuts...
quotes.speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower

quotes.text: A trivial prestige exercise which ignored the social conditions existing in the world.
quotes.speaker: teachers union organizer

quotes.text: frightful waste of public money.
quotes.speaker: British astronomer

claim: Coast-to-coast calls will make life more serious and leave no escape from one's past
what_happened: Long-distance calling proved its use within years (the 1918 pandemic) and became universal
lesson: Connection that ends anonymity is mourned by the press long before people notice they prefer being reachable.

quotes.text: It will be impossible to lose oneself even by joining the Democratic Party.
quotes.speaker: Los Angeles Times

quotes.text: there is a large percentage of the inhabitants of this earth who have never conceded that the telephone in any of its forms, short or long distance, ever was or ever will be a blessing
quotes.speaker: Los Angeles Times

quotes.text: It is bad enough that talk has always been cheap, but this new scheme is carrying it too far.
quotes.speaker: Los Angeles Times

claim: "Photography mania" spreads like a disease and makes people, especially women, vain
what_happened: Photography became universal; the same charge is now made against selfies and Instagram
lesson: Vanity charges follow every self-representation tool; the market is in memory and connection, which critics overlook.

quotes.text: It is impossible to tell over night who may be attacked by photographic mania.
quotes.speaker: Times Union

quotes.text: This lady was one of the first victims of the camera epidemic.
quotes.speaker: Times Union

quotes.text: Only the unthinking consider photography but a handmaid of vanity
quotes.speaker: photography studio advertisement

claim: Ambitious amateur photographers put themselves in danger to get the shot
what_happened: A real but small risk, reborn as selfie deaths ("killfies"); it never slowed adoption
lesson: A real edge-case harm can be true without being a reason to stop; design for the edge without abandoning the core.

quotes.text: Bold invasions of dangerous places made by ambitious amateurs.
quotes.speaker: The New York Times

claim: Retouched photographs lie and feed the vanity of the inordinately vain
what_happened: Retouching became universal (Photoshop, filters); body-image concerns about filters have some research support
lesson: Image manipulation always ships with the camera; trust norms adapt, but some real harm to self-image persists.

quotes.text: Middle aged women who have become slightly obese and count more than one chin now shed their poundage though the aid of the retouchers art.
quotes.speaker: The Journal Times

quotes.text: suit the vanity of the inordinately vain.
quotes.speaker: newspaper

claim: Compulsory mask laws are bunk and an intrusion
what_happened: San Francisco repealed and then reinstated masks within two weeks as cases spiked; the gauze masks of 1918 had limited efficacy, and the fight replayed in 2020
lesson: Resistance to a public-health rule is as much about compulsion as efficacy; the evidence base has to be stronger than the mandate.

quotes.text: All this talk about making the wearing of masks compulsory sounds to me like bunk.
quotes.speaker: President Farmer of the Council

quotes.text: I would rather spend the rest of my life in jail than wear one
quotes.speaker: man refusing mask

claim: A GUI with no command line is cartoony and childish, and students' work suffers on it
what_happened: The GUI became the universal interface
lesson: An interface that lowers the skill floor is always called childish by those who mastered the old one.

thing: Removal of legacy ports and formats (floppy, CD, Flash, USB-A, headphone jack)
claim: Dropping a beloved standard will alienate users and doom the product
what_happened: Each removal (iMac floppy 1998, MacBook Air CD 2008, iPad Flash 2010, USB-C 2015, iPhone 7 jack 2016) was followed by the industry copying it
lesson: Outrage at a removal is loud and brief; if the replacement is genuinely better, the industry follows within a few years.

claim: The new typhoid vaccine is dangerous and should be resisted
what_happened: Military data showed it worked; it was extended to civilians
lesson: Answer resistance with the field data you already have; a dataset beats an argument.

claim: Straining to hear radio gives women "radio face" wrinkles
what_happened: No such condition exists
lesson: A named syndrome is not a diagnosis; most new-device syndromes vanish once the device is ordinary.

quotes.text: The strain of trying to catch every word of wireless broadcast constantly puckers the lines around the sides of her mouth
quotes.speaker: newspaper

claim: Skateboarding is a dangerous childish nuisance to be banned (Norway banned it 1978-1989)
what_happened: Skateboarding became an Olympic sport in 2021
lesson: What authorities treat as a youth nuisance can become a respected institution; the lag is decades, not years.

claim: Jazz is causing a labour shortage on farms
what_happened: The labour shortage had economic causes; jazz became canon
lesson: Blaming the new pastime for a labour shortage is easier than examining wages.

claim: Clocks are now so cheap and abundant that nobody knows the real time
what_happened: Cheap timekeeping enabled modern scheduling and rail travel; commodity status is the sign of success
lesson: When a luxury becomes a commodity, the complaints shift from price to quality and clutter; that is the sound of a market being won.

quotes.text: The more clocks they have the less they know as to what of day or night.
quotes.speaker: Independence Daily Reporter

quotes.text: Clocks come with baking powder, dry goods, cigars, and about everything that is sold... ...none keep the time.
quotes.speaker: Independence Daily Reporter

claim: Selling erotic photographs is an abuse of photography to be punished with jail
what_happened: The trade never stopped; payment-processor and platform pressure on OnlyFans replays the same fight
lesson: Every new image medium immediately serves adult demand; regulation lags and lands on the sellers.

quotes.text: would certainly be paid by their admirers
quotes.speaker: Paris prosecutor (reported)

claim: Computing is a fad that is fading and students are fleeing the field
what_happened: Enrollment dips were cyclical; computing became the dominant career field
lesson: Cyclical dips in a rising field get reported as the end of the field.

quotes.text: STUDENTS FLEE FIELD AS COMPUTER 'FAD FADES'
quotes.speaker: newspaper headline

claim: "Kodak fiends" photograph unwitting people in public, requiring laws against cameras
what_happened: Cameras are everywhere and privacy norms did erode, but cameras also became a check on power (police accountability)
lesson: Privacy fears about cameras are partly right; the winning products build in norms (indicator lights) rather than waiting for laws.

quotes.text: The Kodak fiend may be an abomination to the over-nervous and sensitive, but he will not be a circumstance to the X-ray prowler.
quotes.speaker: The Daily Herald

thing: Camera smart glasses (Google Glass, Ray-Ban Stories)
claim: Camera glasses are creepy surveillance devices
what_happened: Google Glass failed as consumer product partly on this; Meta's glasses later sold, while billions of phone cameras drew little concern
lesson: A visible recording signal is cheap; skipping it can sink a product even when the fear is overstated.

claim: A skeptical nation visits on the airplane the doubts it once felt for the automobile
what_happened: Commercial aviation became the safest mass transport
lesson: Each new vehicle inherits the skepticism of the last one; the arguments barely change.

quotes.text: A Skeptical Nation Visits Upon the Airplane the Doubts it Once Felt for the Automobile
quotes.speaker: The New York Times (subtitle)

claim: Bicycles break up courtship: young men ride off and leave the young ladies
what_happened: Bicycles widened courtship circles (geneticists have linked them to more outbreeding)
lesson: Mobility tools get blamed for disrupting relationships they in fact expand.

quotes.text: It is claimed the young men go off on their wheels and leave the young ladies to themselves.
quotes.speaker: The Kenney Gazette

claim: Explicit music lyrics corrupt children and need Senate hearings and warning labels
what_happened: Parental Advisory stickers became standard; no measurable harm was established and the labels became a marketing badge
lesson: A warning label meant to suppress a product often ends up advertising it.

quotes.text: the twisted tyranny of explicitness in the public domain.
quotes.speaker: Parents Music Resource Center

claim: Violent video games cause youth violence
what_happened: Industry ratings (ESRB) were created; research found no link to real-world violence and the Supreme Court struck down sales bans in 2011
lesson: Self-regulation offered early can defuse a government panic; it rarely stops the hearings.

claim: TV sex and violence drive teen violence, pregnancy and drug use, so every TV needs a censorship chip
what_happened: The V-chip was mandated and almost nobody used it; teen pregnancy and violence fell over following decades
lesson: A mandated control nobody asked for goes unused; demand for safety features has to come from users.

quotes.text: If every parent uses this chip wisely, it can become a powerful voice against teen violence, teen pregnancy, teen drug use, and for both learning and entertainment
quotes.speaker: Bill Clinton

claim: Violent music caused the Columbine shooting
what_happened: The shooters were not even Manson fans; blame shifted to games and then social media
lesson: After a tragedy, the newest youth culture is the first suspect; evidence arrives after the hearings.

quotes.text: devil worshipping maniac
quotes.speaker: politicians and press

claim: Raves are ecstasy dens; promoters and venue owners should be jailed
what_happened: Drug use at raves was real; the RAVE Act failed but passed in another form in 2003, and electronic dance music became mainstream
lesson: A real harm attached to a scene invites liability rules that punish the venue rather than the act.

quotes.text: I'd put the son-of-a-gun in jail.
quotes.speaker: Joe Biden

claim: Radio waves cause illness, droughts, floods and misfortune ("radio black magic")
what_happened: Radio waves were harmless at broadcast power; fakers sold remedies like wire-net underwear
lesson: Invisible technologies attract blame for everything; fakers will sell cures, so explain the mechanism early and plainly.

quotes.text: It is not surprising that “supernatural” powers are attributed to radio waves and that many people have attributed illness, misfortunes and hoodoos to the malevolent influence of radio black magic.
quotes.speaker: The San Francisco Examiner

quotes.text: Radio waves are not a new thing, created by man; the only novelty about the waves is that man has regulated them in such a way as to use them to carry words, music and other signals.
quotes.speaker: The San Francisco Examiner

claim: Aviation is a sickening human sacrifice to science that is not worth the deaths
what_happened: Early flying was genuinely deadly (64 deaths by 1911), but aviation became the safest mode of mass transport
lesson: Early safety records of a new vehicle are real and terrible; the question is whether the curve bends, not where it starts.

quotes.text: IS THIS SICKENING HUMAN SACRIFICE TO SCIENCE WORTH WHILE?
quotes.speaker: newspaper headline

quotes.text: Fools? Victims? Martyrs? Which are they?
quotes.speaker: newspaper

claim: Reports of reactions show the polio vaccine is dangerous
what_happened: Polio cases collapsed after vaccination
lesson: Anecdotes of unproven reactions travel faster than the case-count chart; put the chart next to them.

claim: The Y2K bug will halt the global economy at midnight
what_happened: Little broke, partly because of a large, costly remediation effort; the panic itself was overblown
lesson: A known, dated risk with a patch is manageable; spend on the fix, not the panic.

claim: Nuclear power is too dangerous; phase it out (Germany)
what_happened: Accidents were real, but nuclear has among the lowest deaths per unit of energy; Germany's exit raised coal use and dependence on Russian gas
lesson: Precaution has invisible victims; the cost of not using a technology must be counted alongside its risks.

claim: The Soviet state saw copiers as a threat to its control of publishing and locked them away
what_happened: Copiers stayed behind steel doors until the USSR's last years; democratized copying (samizdat, then the internet) did erode state control
lesson: A gatekeeper who fears that a tool will democratize their monopoly is usually right; that is the opportunity, not the risk.

quotes.text: guarded, double-locked, steel-covered doors.
quotes.speaker: description of Soviet copier controls

claim: Crosswords are a dangerous menace and a waste of time, said the NYT and Times of London
what_happened: Both papers later ran the most famous crosswords in the world; the NYT bought Wordle in 2022
lesson: The publication that sneers at a craze may end up owning its best version; watch what readers pay for.

quotes.text: dealt the final blow to the art of conversations.
quotes.speaker: British newspaper

claim: The mail carries vile publications into homes and corrupts children (Comstock laws)
what_happened: Comstock bans on contraception ads by mail were struck down by the Supreme Court in 1983; the laws now resurface over abortion pills
lesson: A distribution channel that reaches the home bypasses gatekeepers and draws content laws that outlive their era.

quotes.text: The United States Mail is today one of the greatest and most powerful agencies in carrying into the homes, and scattering among the children of the country these vile publications that cannot
quotes.speaker: Anthony Comstock

claim: Teddy bears replacing dolls will suppress maternal instinct and cause race suicide
what_happened: Teddy bears became the classic childhood toy
lesson: A fad toy that changes children's play gets loaded with the anxieties of the day; it says more about the anxiety than the toy.

quotes.text: Race suicide, the gravest danger which confronts this nation today, is being fostered and encouraged by the fad for supplanting the good old dolls of our childhood with the horrible monstrosity known as the ‘Teddy Bear.’
quotes.speaker: Rev. Michael G. Esper

claim: Children's cartoons promote a gay agenda and turn kids gay
what_happened: The claims were ridiculed; the shows remained hits
lesson: Moral panic about kids' entertainment recycles; the target changes, the script does not.

claim: 5G will massively increase the population's exposure to harmful radiation
what_happened: No health effects were found; by 2020 the same paper was debunking 5G-coronavirus conspiracies
lesson: Respectable outlets can seed a fear that later becomes a conspiracy theory; framing matters from the start.

quotes.text: the Internet of Things will require augmenting today’s 4G technology with 5G technology, thus “massively increasing” the general population’s exposure to radiation
quotes.speaker: The Guardian

claim: The home PC is a fad headed the way of the hula hoop and video games; there is no home computer market
what_happened: PCs and then pocket networked computers became universal; amateur video, which Weizenbaum used as his counterexample, now dominates them
lesson: Micro pessimism about today's form factor is usually right; macro pessimism about the idea is usually wrong. Judge the category, not the beta.

quotes.text: I quite disagree. I think that won’t work.
quotes.speaker: Joseph Weizenbaum

quotes.text: The home computer may be going the way of video games, which are a dying fad
quotes.speaker: Steve Wozniak

quotes.text: One of them is that there is such a thing as the home computer market. It doesn't exist.
quotes.speaker: John Sculley

claim: Office work is an unnatural habitat; office men must go hunting to stay sane
what_happened: Office work became the norm; the sedentary health costs were real, and the debate replays over remote work
lesson: Every new way of working is called unnatural; some of the costs are real and become a market of their own.

claim: Glasgow Town Council refused permission for the first horseless carriage on its streets
what_happened: Cars arrived in thousands; Glasgow later made its subway fully autonomous
lesson: Permission denied locally is a delay, not a verdict; regulators eventually license what the public adopts.

quotes.text: Those in authority might as well try to beat back the waves of the sea with a broom as try to stem the tide of horseless carriage which are looming in the distance.
quotes.speaker: applicant for horseless carriage permit

claim: New inventions cause typewriter back, telephone ear, motor eye and other ailments
what_happened: Most "ailments" were invented, but repetitive strain injury was real and is still treated
lesson: Among a list of imagined harms there is usually one real one; find it and design for it instead of dismissing the list.

quotes.text: Twentieth century inventions are changing he normal human into an abnormal specimen - cogs of flesh and bone to fit smoothly into cogs of steel and iron.
quotes.speaker: St. Louis Post-Dispatch

claim: Televising the coronation would make a sacred ceremony a theatrical performance
what_happened: Public outcry overturned the ban; 27 million watched and TV sales boomed
lesson: Institutions that refuse a new medium for dignity's sake get overruled by the public they serve; access wins.

quotes.text: It would be unfitting that the whole ceremony, not only in its secular but also in its religious and spiritual aspects, should be presented as if it were a theatrical performance.
quotes.speaker: Winston Churchill

claim: Photography means painting is dead
what_happened: Painting survived and reinvented itself (impressionism, abstraction), mostly using photos as an aide, though miniature portrait trades shrank
lesson: A new medium kills the commodity version of a craft and pushes the craft toward what the machine cannot do.

quotes.text: From today, painting is dead.
quotes.speaker: Paul Delaroche (attributed)

claim: Sundials chop days wretchedly into small portions and make people eat by the clock
what_happened: The lament was likely satire in a Plautus comedy; timekeeping became the basis of civilization
lesson: Complaints about tools that structure our time are older than writing about them; even the ancients mocked them.

quotes.text: To cut and hack my days so wretchedly
quotes.speaker: Plautus (character)

claim: Bicycling causes insanity and deformities of the spine and face; insurers refused cyclists
what_happened: Cycling is now prescribed for health
lesson: When physicians and insurers both warn against something new, check whether they measured the harm or priced in the unfamiliarity.

claim: Roller skating deforms limbs, stunts children and empties churches
what_happened: Roller skating became a harmless mass pastime
lesson: Leisure that competes with church on Sunday gets a health warning attached.

claim: Students will use ChatGPT to cheat, so schools must block it
what_happened: NYC banned ChatGPT in January 2023 and reversed within months; schools now debate how to teach with it, echoing earlier bans on MySpace and smartphones
lesson: Schools that ban the tool of the future job market end up teaching it a few years later; build for the reversal.

thing: Electronic calculators and computers (replacing the slide rule)
claim: Without the slide rule, students lose a sense of magnitude and the concepts behind calculation
what_happened: The slide rule became obsolete; the same argument now targets AI in classrooms
lesson: "They will lose the underlying skill" is said of every tool that automates a skill; the skill that matters moves up a level.

quotes.text: The slide rule's demise is viewed with serious regret by many teachers, technicians and scientists.
quotes.speaker: newspaper

quotes.text: You can program a computer to perform a certain task, then you can train anybody to punch numbers into it. But if you don't teach him the concepts, how will he learn to program the computer himself?
quotes.speaker: John Strack, physics teacher

claim: The internet lets students submit ready-made, paid-for essays
what_happened: Contract cheating is real and grew, but detection and assessment adapted; the debate restarted with ChatGPT
lesson: A real cheating risk changes how work is assessed rather than stopping the tool.

quotes.text: Is this a student's work I see before me - or just a ready-made, paid-for download from the internet?
quotes.speaker: The Guardian

claim: Sampling is theft of artists' work
what_happened: Courts forced sampling into a licensing regime (from 1991), and sampling-based hip hop became dominant
lesson: A new remix technology usually ends in a licensing market, not a ban; position for the licence.

claim: Typewritten love letters are cold, mechanical and unromantic
what_happened: Keyboards replaced pens for most writing; a typed letter now reads as a romantic gesture
lesson: Writing tools always get accused of killing sincerity; the sentiment survives the medium.

quotes.text: cold-blooded, mechanical, unromantic production imaginable
quotes.speaker: newspaper writer

quotes.text: The girl who will put up with a typewritten love letter will put up with anything.
quotes.speaker: newspaper writer

quotes.text: Love uses the telephone, whispers at 50 cents a word to the Atlantic cable, and displays itself without fear or punctuation upon yellow telegraph blanks; why then should it hesitate in the presence of a typewriting machine?
quotes.speaker: newspaper editor

claim: Fraudulent photographs enable slander and fraud and must be federally banned
what_happened: Fake photos did enable fraud, blackmail and fake nudes; the broad 1912 bill died, and the same debate returned with Photoshop and AI
lesson: Regulate the specific proven harm (fake nudes, fraud), not the whole technique; broad bans die and leave the real harm unaddressed.

quotes.text: ...at the present time photographs may be and are made to lie with great frequency and facility.
quotes.speaker: New-York Tribune

quotes.text: miserable business of creating fake photographs
quotes.speaker: Intelligencer Journal

quotes.text: Their methods are to get possession of the photographs of well known and prominent society women and then attach to the head of the picture the photograph of the half or whole of a nude body.
quotes.speaker: The Topeka State Journal

claim: Machines eliminating human labour caused the Great Depression
what_happened: Mass technological unemployment did not persist; Einstein had fallen for the lump-of-labour fallacy, and the narrative may have deepened the slump
lesson: Job-loss narratives can depress demand by themselves; be careful which story you amplify about your own technology.

quotes.text: the improvement in the apparatus of production through technical invention and organization has decreased the need for human labor
quotes.speaker: Albert Einstein

quotes.text: Einstein Traces Slump to Machine
quotes.speaker: The New York Times (headline)

thing: Radio news (War of the Worlds broadcast)
claim: Radio is an irresponsible medium that panics the public and is not fit to deliver news
what_happened: The mass panic was largely invented by newspapers losing ad revenue to radio; radio became a trusted news source
lesson: When the old medium reports on the new one's dangers, it is also reporting on its own competitor.

quotes.text: The nation as a whole continues to face the danger of incomplete, misunderstood news over a medium which has yet to prove ... that it is competent to perform the news job.
quotes.speaker: Editor and Publisher

quotes.text: A wave of mass hysteria seized thousands of radio listeners throughout the nation.
quotes.speaker: The New York Times

claim: A popular novel glorifying suicide will cause young readers to kill themselves
what_happened: Bans followed in Italy, Denmark and parts of Germany; of 19 suicides blamed on it only 2 could be tied to the book, though media-driven suicide contagion (the "Werther effect") is real for news coverage
lesson: Owning a popular product is not evidence it caused a tragedy; but how a harm is reported can create the contagion it fears.

quotes.text: we would wish that it had never been written.
quotes.speaker: German newspaper review (translated)

quotes.text: caused more suicides than the most beautiful woman in the world
quotes.speaker: author (1813)

claim: Magazines spread a "brain-rot contagion" so people think in little broken thoughts
what_happened: Magazines became a respected medium; "brainrot" is now aimed at short-form video
lesson: "Brainrot" is a century-old charge from the old medium against the new one; judge attention claims by evidence, not vocabulary.

quotes.text: The number of people who think like birds, in little broken thoughts, will be greatly enlarged.
quotes.speaker: Julian Ralph

quotes.text: The best of them are brain-rotting trash and twaddle, and the worst of them are deadly poison.
quotes.speaker: The Press (Stafford Springs)

claim: Constant radio listening softens the brain ("radio perpetuum"), hurts grades and kills birds
what_happened: Radio's feared harms (dead birds, poor grades, sleep loss) were unfounded
lesson: A disease name coined by a critic is a rhetorical device, not a diagnosis.

quotes.text: Persons who listen to the radio from dawn to dusk suffer from the disease “radio perpetuum”, a slow but sure softening of the brain
quotes.speaker: a preacher

claim: Chess is an inferior amusement that robs the mind of valuable time and may harm players' sanity
what_happened: Chess is now treated as brain training
lesson: A pastime called a waste of time in one century can be the model of virtue in the next.

quotes.text: Chess is a mere amusement of a very inferior character, which robs the mind of valuable time
quotes.speaker: Scientific American

thing: Recorded sound in movie theaters ("canned music")
claim: Canned music will banish live musicians and art itself
what_happened: Theatre musician jobs did disappear, but Hollywood recording musicians earned concert wages; the union spent $9M fighting the inevitable and capped its own members' hours
lesson: A union can be right that a job category shrinks and still lose by fighting it instead of capturing the new work.

quotes.text: Is Art to Have a Tyrant?
quotes.speaker: American Federation of Musicians ad

quotes.text: Local musicians are making, for the first time in their lives, concert artists’ wages recording this very ‘canned music’ against which their less fortunately situated brethren are protesting.
quotes.speaker: newspaper

claim: Secure communication without a pre-shared secret key is obviously impossible, and GCHQ doubted its own invention
what_happened: GCHQ kept it classified; Stanford and MIT rediscovered it and it now secures the internet for billions
lesson: Institutions that sit on a breakthrough out of caution hand the credit and the market to outsiders.

quotes.text: It was obvious to everyone, including me," he later wrote, "that no secure communication was possible without a secret key
quotes.speaker: James Ellis

claim: Public encryption must be outlawed, export-controlled or backdoored with government-held keys
what_happened: PGP spread beyond control; the UK backed down in 1999, US controls eased and encryption became the internet's backbone, though governments keep pushing backdoors
lesson: Open-sourcing a capability can make control impossible; regulators then have to accept it.

claim: Long-distance carriers petitioned the FCC to ban internet telephony as unfair competition
what_happened: The FCC sat on the petition for 8 years and in 2004 allowed free internet calling, now universal
lesson: Incumbents use old rules to block new competition; a scrappy coalition can stall them long enough for the market to decide.

quotes.text: Are we hurting their ability to charge you $10 for a long-distance phone call? Tough bananas
quotes.speaker: Harvey Kaufman, NetSpeak

quotes.text: But Marc Andreessen, Netscape Corp.'s technology guru, said his Mountain View-based company will make computer-to-computer voice capability a standard feature in the next version of its browser program.
quotes.speaker: The San Francisco Examiner

claim: An inordinate passion for novels poisons young minds and ruins education
what_happened: Novels became a core of education
lesson: Even the greatest minds of an era fall for "kids these days"; brilliance in one field is no protection.

quotes.text: A great obstacle to good education is the inordinate passion prevalent for novels
quotes.speaker: Thomas Jefferson

quotes.text: the result is a bloated imagination, sickly judgment, and disgust towards all the real businesses of life.
quotes.speaker: Thomas Jefferson

claim: A man who thinks he can make ice is a crank playing God
what_happened: Gorrie's 1851 patent began modern refrigeration
lesson: Making a natural product artificially sounds like playing God until it is cheaper.

quotes.text: There is a Dr. Gorrie, a crank, down in Florida, who thinks he can make ice as good as God Almighty.
quotes.speaker: The New York Daily Globe (reported)

claim: Natural ice is purer and science cannot beat nature
what_happened: Natural ice declined by the 1930s despite certification labels; artificial won on purity because lakes were polluted
lesson: An incumbent's "natural" label can slow a manufactured rival but rarely stops it; bans can, which is why lab-meat bans matter.

quotes.text: Science Fails and We Must All Bow Our Head to Nature
quotes.speaker: natural ice advertisement

claim: Personal headphones withdraw people from society into an airtight bubble
what_happened: The Walkman became a nostalgic icon; personal audio is universal
lesson: Products that let individuals control their environment are called antisocial before they are called essential.

quotes.text: a nonstop... masturbational fantasy
quotes.speaker: Allan Bloom
quotes.publication: The Closing of the American Mind

quotes.text: Of all the saddening signs of a troubled society, I saw perhaps the most chilling of all the other afternoon. There, on the midway of the Ohio State Fair, strolled teenagers wearing sony walkman headphones.
quotes.speaker: newspaper columnist

thing: Sony Walkman (headphones while driving or walking)
claim: Headphones block hearing and cause road accidents; towns banned them even for crossing the street
what_happened: Real accidents occurred and some driving restrictions stuck; the jail-threat pedestrian bans (Woodbridge NJ) were mocked and faded
lesson: A narrow, real safety risk justifies narrow rules (driving), not bans on ordinary use.

quotes.text: No municipality has the right to tell somebody what they can wear.
quotes.speaker: Oscar Gross

claim: A rocket cannot work in a vacuum
what_happened: The NYT issued a correction as Apollo 11 approached the moon in 1969
lesson: Confident dismissals from authorities who misunderstand the physics can stand for decades; the correction comes only when the result is undeniable.

claim: Heavy metal spreads Satanism and drives teens to suicide
what_happened: Suicide lawsuits (Ozzy, Judas Priest) were dismissed; the McMartin satanic abuse case collapsed in 1990; Ozzy became a sitcom dad
lesson: In uncertain times people invent demons; the scapegoat ends up a beloved icon.

quotes.text: They live their lives in fear and insecurity... the ministry of fear that won’t let you live.
quotes.speaker: Ozzy Osbourne

thing: Free legal advice over radio ("Good Will Court")
claim: Free legal advice on radio exploits human misery and is contrary to the public interest
what_happened: Bar associations got it banned and the top-10 show went off air; the same fight is now over AI legal aid
lesson: When a profession calls free access to its expertise "contrary to the public interest," check who loses the fees.

quotes.text: unqualifiedly disapproved and condemned as being contrary to public interest.
quotes.speaker: American Bar Association

quotes.text: human misery for commercial purposes
quotes.speaker: Chicago Bar Association

quotes.text: if such a force as this for social betterment is contrary to law, then there is something wrong with the law.
quotes.speaker: memorandum in defense of the show

claim: Freely releasing an automated vulnerability scanner will wreck the internet in a sea of information anarchy
what_happened: The internet was not wrecked; it also did not become as secure as hoped. The same debate now surrounds AI vulnerability finders like MYTHOS
lesson: Dual-use tools released openly tend to strengthen defenders as much as attackers; doom predictions about one release rarely survive a month.

quotes.text: I THINK WE’RE ON THE VERGE OF SEEING THE INTERNET COMPLETELY WRECKED IN A SEA OF INFORMATION ANARCHY.
quotes.speaker: Donn Parker

quotes.text: IT’S LIKE RANDOMLY MAILING AUTOMATIC RIFLES TO 5,000 ADDRESSES. YOU HOPE SOME CRAZY TEEN DOESN’T GET A HOLD OF ONE.
quotes.speaker: Paul Cubbage, Dataquest

claim: A proof checked by computer is not mathematics and cannot be trusted
what_happened: Computer-assisted and formally verified proofs became accepted (the theorem was machine-verified in 2005); the split was largely by age
lesson: Experts often reject a machine-made result on grounds of meaning rather than correctness; the next generation accepts it.

quotes.text: the present proof relies in effect on an Oracle, and I say down with Oracles! They are not mathematics
quotes.speaker: Paul Halmos

quotes.text: God wouldn’t let the theorem be proved by a method as terrible as that!
quotes.speaker: Herbert Wilf

quotes.text: It is the most ridiculous case of ‘The King’s New Clothes’ that has ever disgraced the history of mathematics
quotes.speaker: George Spencer-Brown
